medical.title: Large meta-analysis sheds new light on how SGLT2 inhibitors affect blood and iron parameters
medical.summary: Research led by internist-nephrologist Dr. Michele Eisenga shows that SGLT2 inhibitors, a class of drugs widely used to treat type 2 diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease, consistently increase hemoglobin and hematocrit levels.

medical.title: Airborne ESKAPE pathogens at inner-city clinic resist advanced antibiotics
medical.summary: At a clinic in South Africa, researchers have identified airborne ESKAPE bacteria that survive most antibiotic medicines. The clinic is in a densely populated inner-city area.

medical.title: Shared framework aims to redefine heart health for girls and women
medical.summary: The American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine have released a publication that redefines heart health in girls and women. The organizations together outline four distinct "Female Life Stages" offering women and health care professionals a chance to have heart health conversations from puberty through menopause and beyond.

medical.title: Rare gene variants linked to dental differences that shape our smiles
medical.summary: Rare variants in a gene involved in early development have been linked to a range of dental differences in people, including missing teeth, unusual tooth shapes and teeth present at birth. By studying changes in the same gene in mice and chickens, researchers have also uncovered clues to how differences in tooth number and shape evolved across species, including how birds may have lost their teeth.

medical.title: Personalized cancer vaccine plus immunotherapy reduces melanoma recurrence after surgery
medical.summary: Adding a personalized mRNA-based cancer vaccine to immunotherapy after surgery for high-risk melanoma reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 42%, according to results from the phase 3 INTerpath-001 trial presented at the ESMO Congress 2026. The vaccine, intismeran autogene, was given alongside pembrolizumab and compared with pembrolizumab alone.

medical.title: Small deep brain structure may play major role in sustaining working memory, mouse experiments suggest
medical.summary: Reading a sentence, following a conversation, solving a problem or deciding what to do next: all of these rely on working memory. It allows the brain to hold information in mind for a few seconds, even after the stimulus has disappeared, to be able to compare it with new information, manipulate it and use it to guide our behavior. It therefore plays an essential role in the transition from perception to thought, and from thought to action.

medical.title: Patients given apalutamide and hormone therapy around surgery may cut their risk of metastasis or death
medical.summary: An international phase 3 clinical trial that treated patients with high-risk localized and locally advanced prostate cancer with apalutamide—a next-generation neoadjuvant androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI)—plus hormone therapy before and after prostate cancer surgery was further validated by a substudy demonstrating a reduced risk of metastasis or death compared with standard of care.

medical.title: How daylight saving time changes affect you and what you can do about it
medical.summary: An extra hour of sleep is on the way for most Americans, though the "fall back" to standard time will bring darker afternoons, too.

medical.title: New targeted therapy improved survival for patients with KRAS-mutated lung cancer
medical.summary: Patients with previously treated advanced KRAS G12C-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) lived significantly longer and saw improved disease control when treated with the next-generation KRAS-targeted therapy divarasib, according to researchers from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

medical.title: Weight-loss surgery produces lasting diabetes remission, long-term study finds
medical.summary: People with type 2 diabetes were much more likely to achieve remission after weight-loss surgery than after intensive medical and lifestyle management, according to a long-term study. Researchers also identified patient characteristics linked to remission and to the likelihood of diabetes returning.

medical.title: Are you dressed yet? How parents can build child‑friendly routines that kids can follow
medical.summary: "Please go brush your teeth, get dressed and brush your hair." These are familiar morning requests that parents make to preschool and school-age children.

medical.title: Added antibody step improves the reliability of Alzheimer's blood tests
medical.summary: Researchers at University Medicine Halle have developed a new method that could improve the reliability of blood tests for Alzheimer's disease. Current commercial tests often rely on the protein biomarker p-tau217, whose levels can rise in the early stages of the disease. However, the biomarker levels can also be elevated in other conditions, potentially leading to false-positive results. In a study involving 315 participants, the research team demonstrated improved accuracy in distinguishing Alzheimer's disease from other conditions. Their findings have been published in Nature Communications.

medical.title: Location of rare cancer impacts survival, study suggests
medical.summary: A rare, aggressive cancer, commonly found in the uterus, limbs and abdomen, behaves differently depending on where it is found in the body, according to new research.

medical.title: Viagra's cousin could help muscle cells stay primed for regeneration
medical.summary: Tadalafil is a prescription drug closely related to Viagra. It is used to treat erectile dysfunction (ED) and the urinary symptoms of an enlarged prostate. Both competitive and recreational athletes sometimes use it too, to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), a condition that can limit how well the body tolerates exercise.

medical.title: Tired, irritable and craving carbs? Why darker days affect our bodies and brains
medical.summary: When the clocks go back in October, millions of Britons welcome an extra hour in bed. But by the evening, with darkness arriving before many people finish work, that small luxury may seem a distant memory.

medical.title: One violin lesson changes brain wave patterns as beginners learn to play
medical.summary: A new study using wearable brain imaging has shown what happens in the human brain when someone learns to play a musical instrument. The results revealed the patterns of brain activity that enable us to play an instrument, in this case a violin, and how having just a single lesson significantly changes those patterns of activity.

medical.title: New treatment approach shows promise in reducing prostate cancer spread
medical.summary: Adding darolutamide to standard treatment for aggressive prostate cancer reduced the risk of the disease spreading in an international phase 3 trial.

medical.title: Fructose slows liver tumors in mice when key sugar-processing gene is missing, may lead to new treatments
medical.summary: Fructose is an important nutrient that, despite having a chemical structure very similar to that of glucose, is metabolized very differently in the body. Research into fructose metabolism and its regulation of metabolism in the human body has in recent years become a frontier topic in the life sciences and medicine. A new study led by researchers at City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK) has found that in the specific metabolic context of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), dietary fructose does not fuel tumor growth. Instead, it can suppress it, revealing a previously unknown anticancer mechanism.

medical.title: Previously unrecognized immune cells may drive harmful blood vessel growth in blinding eye diseases
medical.summary: A Northwestern Medicine study has identified a previously unrecognized population of immune cells that appears to fuel harmful blood vessel growth in multiple blinding eye diseases, according to the study published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation. The discovery could open the door to new treatments for patients who don't respond to existing therapies, said the study's senior author Jeremy Lavine, M.D., Ph.D., assistant professor of ophthalmology.

medical.title: Immunotherapy combo extends survival for patients with aggressive small cell lung cancer, based on trial results
medical.summary: In patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC), tarlatamab, a bispecific T-cell engager, plus durvalumab as first-line maintenance therapy extended median overall survival by more than eight months, more than tripled progression-free survival and reduced the risk of death by 58% compared to durvalumab alone, according to results of the phase 3 open-label, multicenter, randomized DeLLphi-305 study.

medical.title: Florida dengue cases nearly double a month after emergency declared
medical.summary: Dengue cases in Florida keep climbing about a month after three counties declared states of emergency over the mosquito-borne illness.

medical.title: AI chatbots may worsen symptoms in people with psychosis
medical.summary: Conversational AI chatbots are a relatively new technology, but they are now ubiquitous, embedded in everything from customer service platforms to personal productivity tools. Such is their rapid adoption that potential negative consequences are yet to be fully understood.

medical.title: AI chatbots can be a valuable health resource for older adults—if they embrace 'informed skepticism'
medical.summary: It's easy to stereotype older adults as tech-averse or novice tech users. Yet a growing number of adults age 60 and older are embracing artificial intelligence, using it for entertainment, planning trips and even accessing health information.

science.title: Freshwater flows reshape Coorong algae communities, 16 years of data reveal
science.summary: Ongoing research is providing a clearer picture of how climate change can affect different aspects of the Coorong in South Australia—and is helping develop strong environmental strategies that can be adapted as the climate changes.

science.title: Could ecological roles offer clues to how life began?
science.summary: Producers, consumers, and decomposers play different roles in today's ecosystems. Thinking about these familiar roles led me to a question: Could their differences partly reflect the different physical and chemical environments in which early life developed? I wondered whether the organization of ecosystems might offer a useful starting point for thinking about life's beginnings.

science.title: Expanding hemp could boost Kentucky water quality and ecological diversity
science.summary: Hemp has long been pitched to Kentucky farmers as a way to diversify their income. Research now suggests it could diversify the landscape itself, with measurable benefits for the state's water and wildlife.

science.title: Metalens microscope switches focus with voltage, not moving optics
science.summary: Just as it is difficult for a camera to keep both a nearby flower and a distant mountain sharply focused at the same time, conventional optical microscopes face a similar challenge when imaging structures located at different depths inside the body. Tighter focusing of light improves spatial resolution, but at the same time reduces the depth range over which the image remains sharply focused.

science.title: Beyond trial and error: Integrating computation, processing, and AI to design high-entropy alloys
science.summary: Designing structural high-entropy alloys (SHEAs) means solving a problem with an enormous number of moving parts: which combinations of composition and processing conditions will yield the phases, microstructures, and mechanical properties a given application demands? Because these alloys mix multiple principal elements in comparable proportions, that question spans length and time scales that no single experiment or model can cover on its own.

The rover’s “eyes” captured a very exciting geologic feature during its traverse — a contact between distinct rock […]

science.title: NASA’s Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust
science.summary: Over 1,645 Martian days, NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover measured the fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles found clinging to samples of spacesuit materials that are carried aboard the rover, including some that are small enough to penetrate the lungs and enter the bloodstream. The findings will be published Tuesday, Oct. 27, in the Proceedings of […]

science.title: Silent bacterial genes yield potential leads for future cancer drugs
science.summary: Natural products produced by microorganisms are a promising source of new drugs. Researchers at the Helmholtz Center for Infection Research (HZI) and its Saarbrücken-based site, the Helmholtz Institute for Pharmaceutical Research Saarland (HIPS), have now discovered a new family of such compounds, elucidated their unusual biosynthesis and developed a way to produce them synthetically.

science.title: NEO Surveyor’s Sunshade Gets Inspected
science.summary: Description The large sunshade of NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor is mounted on an assembly ring during inspections in a clean room at BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems in Boulder, Colorado, in July 2026. The sunshade structure stands 20 feet (6 meters) tall and measures 8 feet (2.4 meters) wide at its base. Its two flat […]

science.summary: Description The large sunshade of NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor mission is inspected by a technician at BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems in Boulder, Colorado, in late July. Built by Applied Aerospace in Stockton, California, the sunshade structure was outfitted with its solar cells by SolAero Technologies in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in January. Environmental […]

science.title: Can cats really thrive on vegan diets? Professor Andrew Knight responds to critics
science.summary: In response to a recent article on vegan diets for cats, Phys.org received numerous messages from concerned readers. People raised a lot of concerns, mainly arguing that cats are obligate carnivores and that vegan diets could be very harmful to their health. Now, we have collected all these comments, questions and concerns and asked the researcher behind the original paper to address them. Andrew Knight, Veterinary Professor of Animal Welfare and Associate Professor at Murdoch University School of Veterinary Medicine, offers his response below.

science.title: Tree‑hugging optional: What today's green tradespeople actually care about
science.summary: Is masculinity a barrier to green jobs?

science.title: Single optical element combines soft X-ray imaging and spectroscopy
science.summary: An international research team from Germany, Switzerland and Japan has demonstrated in a recent study that a single reflection zone plate (RZP) can perform both soft X-ray imaging and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) mapping. The approach could simplify future instruments that need to determine both where structures are located in a material and how their electronic properties vary.

science.title: Simulations reveal design rules for high-performance DNA particle motors
science.summary: DNA-nano/microparticle motors are among the fastest artificial molecular motors reported to date, moving at approximately 30 nm per second. However, they are still slower than natural motor proteins (approximately 100–1,000 nm per second), and further improvements in design and performance are required.

science.title: Shared aquifers, border hotspots: Cooperation should follow where groundwater is pumped, scientists say
science.summary: Groundwater depletion and groundwater-dependent irrigation tend to concentrate close to international borders within aquifers shared by two or more countries, where pumping on one side is more likely to affect users on the other, according to a publication by the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH).

science.title: Keeping water molecules connected reduces carbon electrode corrosion
science.summary: Carbon is inexpensive, conductive, and widely used in technologies such as fuel cells and water electrolyzers. But under strongly oxidizing conditions, carbon electrodes gradually corrode.

science.title: Hydrogen production from seawater: Low-cost catalyst could cut energy use and resist corrosion
science.summary: Using a range of advanced characterization techniques, researchers say they have developed a novel method with the potential to produce hydrogen from seawater using a process that requires less energy, resists corrosion and could support more economical hydrogen production.

science.title: Botanists comb Gabon's rich rainforests with nature on the line
science.summary: Each year, Gabon's lush rainforests yield the discovery of previously unknown plant species to botanists like Archange Boupoya—who believes that this exceptional yet largely mysterious natural wealth needs to be cataloged to be saved.

science.title: What is 'human composting'—and how does it work?
science.summary: What should happen to your body after you die? It's hardly a topic you'd bring up over dinner, but it's a decision that will eventually need to be made, either by you or by those you leave behind.

science.title: Scientists produce less disruptive research as they age, but their breakthroughs are more likely to last
science.summary: Science often advances in small steps, with researchers gradually building on previous discoveries. But every now and then, a breakthrough comes along that challenges conventional thinking and changes the direction of a field.

science.title: NASA SEES Interns Tackle Real-World Challenges in Lunar Exploration
science.summary: The NASA STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) Enhancement in Earth Science (SEES) Internship Program at the University of Texas Center for Space Research places high school students on small, mission-focused research teams mentored by NASA, academic, and industry experts. During summer 2026, the SEES Mission Architecture Tool for Research, Integration, and eXploration (MATRIX) team […]

science.title: Hidden chromosome structures reveal greater complexity in how roundworms organize DNA
science.summary: Almost every cell in our body contains around two meters (6.6 feet) of DNA, packed into a tiny nucleus. Yet for the cell to function, this enormous amount of genetic material must remain organized and accessible. Researchers at the University of Basel have now discovered three distinct types of large chromosomal domains that help organize DNA in nuclei.

science.title: The power of poop: Why conservationists love animal scat
science.summary: I never thought my shoelaces would get stolen.

science.title: AI-powered robotic laboratory paves the way for discovering next-generation heat-resistant coatings
science.summary: Researchers have developed a self-driving laboratory that combines artificial intelligence and robotics to automate laboratory tasks, from accurately measuring and mixing chemical ingredients to high-temperature furnace processing and sample retrieval.

science.title: Two distinct sleep stages emerge in jumping spider, including a REM-like state
science.summary: Humans and other vertebrates go through various stages of sleep, including REM (rapid eye movement) sleep characterized by rapid eye movements and muscle twitches. Can a similar sleep state be observed in spiders? Researchers from the Institute of Organismic Biology at the University of Bonn investigated this in the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata. The work is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

environment.title: Governors allied with Flávio Bolsonaro set to lead majority of Brazilian Amazon states
environment.summary: Seven of Brazil’s nine Amazonian states are set to be governed by politicians aligned with far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, Lucas Berti reported for Mongabay Brasil. On Oct. 25, Brazil will have an electoral face-off between the top two candidates for several races that were not able to secure more than 50% of the vote in […]

environment.title: Inside the ‘unique’ tail of Iran’s spider-tailed horned viper
environment.summary: The Iranian spider-tailed horned viper, a rare snake endemic to western Iran, hunts by holding its body completely still while twitching its tail. The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

environment.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
environment.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

environment.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
environment.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

environment.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
environment.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

environment.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
environment.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

environment.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
environment.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.

mix_items.title: Could ecological roles offer clues to how life began?
mix_items.summary: Producers, consumers, and decomposers play different roles in today's ecosystems. Thinking about these familiar roles led me to a question: Could their differences partly reflect the different physical and chemical environments in which early life developed? I wondered whether the organization of ecosystems might offer a useful starting point for thinking about life's beginnings.

mix_items.title: Airborne ESKAPE pathogens at inner-city clinic resist advanced antibiotics
mix_items.summary: At a clinic in South Africa, researchers have identified airborne ESKAPE bacteria that survive most antibiotic medicines. The clinic is in a densely populated inner-city area.

mix_items.title: Shared framework aims to redefine heart health for girls and women
mix_items.summary: The American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine have released a publication that redefines heart health in girls and women. The organizations together outline four distinct "Female Life Stages" offering women and health care professionals a chance to have heart health conversations from puberty through menopause and beyond.

mix_items.title: Expanding hemp could boost Kentucky water quality and ecological diversity
mix_items.summary: Hemp has long been pitched to Kentucky farmers as a way to diversify their income. Research now suggests it could diversify the landscape itself, with measurable benefits for the state's water and wildlife.

mix_items.title: Rare gene variants linked to dental differences that shape our smiles
mix_items.summary: Rare variants in a gene involved in early development have been linked to a range of dental differences in people, including missing teeth, unusual tooth shapes and teeth present at birth. By studying changes in the same gene in mice and chickens, researchers have also uncovered clues to how differences in tooth number and shape evolved across species, including how birds may have lost their teeth.

mix_items.title: Metalens microscope switches focus with voltage, not moving optics
mix_items.summary: Just as it is difficult for a camera to keep both a nearby flower and a distant mountain sharply focused at the same time, conventional optical microscopes face a similar challenge when imaging structures located at different depths inside the body. Tighter focusing of light improves spatial resolution, but at the same time reduces the depth range over which the image remains sharply focused.

mix_items.title: Personalized cancer vaccine plus immunotherapy reduces melanoma recurrence after surgery
mix_items.summary: Adding a personalized mRNA-based cancer vaccine to immunotherapy after surgery for high-risk melanoma reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 42%, according to results from the phase 3 INTerpath-001 trial presented at the ESMO Congress 2026. The vaccine, intismeran autogene, was given alongside pembrolizumab and compared with pembrolizumab alone.

mix_items.title: Beyond trial and error: Integrating computation, processing, and AI to design high-entropy alloys
mix_items.summary: Designing structural high-entropy alloys (SHEAs) means solving a problem with an enormous number of moving parts: which combinations of composition and processing conditions will yield the phases, microstructures, and mechanical properties a given application demands? Because these alloys mix multiple principal elements in comparable proportions, that question spans length and time scales that no single experiment or model can cover on its own.

mix_items.title: Small deep brain structure may play major role in sustaining working memory, mouse experiments suggest
mix_items.summary: Reading a sentence, following a conversation, solving a problem or deciding what to do next: all of these rely on working memory. It allows the brain to hold information in mind for a few seconds, even after the stimulus has disappeared, to be able to compare it with new information, manipulate it and use it to guide our behavior. It therefore plays an essential role in the transition from perception to thought, and from thought to action.

mix_items.title: Silent bacterial genes yield potential leads for future cancer drugs

Researchers at the Helmholtz Center for Infection Research (HZI) and its Saarbrücken-based site, the Helmholtz Institute for Pharmaceutical Research Saarland (HIPS), have now discovered a new family of such compounds, elucidated their unusual biosynthesis and developed a way to produce them synthetically.

mix_items.summary: Patients with previously treated advanced KRAS G12C-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) lived significantly longer and saw improved disease control when treated with the next-generation KRAS-targeted therapy divarasib, according to researchers from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

mix_items.title: Single optical element combines soft X-ray imaging and spectroscopy
mix_items.summary: An international research team from Germany, Switzerland and Japan has demonstrated in a recent study that a single reflection zone plate (RZP) can perform both soft X-ray imaging and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) mapping. The approach could simplify future instruments that need to determine both where structures are located in a material and how their electronic properties vary.

mix_items.title: Weight-loss surgery produces lasting diabetes remission, long-term study finds
mix_items.summary: People with type 2 diabetes were much more likely to achieve remission after weight-loss surgery than after intensive medical and lifestyle management, according to a long-term study. Researchers also identified patient characteristics linked to remission and to the likelihood of diabetes returning.

mix_items.title: Are you dressed yet? How parents can build child‑friendly routines that kids can follow
mix_items.summary: "Please go brush your teeth, get dressed and brush your hair." These are familiar morning requests that parents make to preschool and school-age children.

mix_items.title: Simulations reveal design rules for high-performance DNA particle motors
mix_items.summary: DNA-nano/microparticle motors are among the fastest artificial molecular motors reported to date, moving at approximately 30 nm per second. However, they are still slower than natural motor proteins (approximately 100–1,000 nm per second), and further improvements in design and performance are required.

mix_items.title: Shared aquifers, border hotspots: Cooperation should follow where groundwater is pumped, scientists say
mix_items.summary: Groundwater depletion and groundwater-dependent irrigation tend to concentrate close to international borders within aquifers shared by two or more countries, where pumping on one side is more likely to affect users on the other, according to a publication by the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH).

mix_items.title: Keeping water molecules connected reduces carbon electrode corrosion
mix_items.summary: Carbon is inexpensive, conductive, and widely used in technologies such as fuel cells and water electrolyzers. But under strongly oxidizing conditions, carbon electrodes gradually corrode.

mix_items.title: Hydrogen production from seawater: Low-cost catalyst could cut energy use and resist corrosion
mix_items.summary: Using a range of advanced characterization techniques, researchers say they have developed a novel method with the potential to produce hydrogen from seawater using a process that requires less energy, resists corrosion and could support more economical hydrogen production.

mix_items.title: Added antibody step improves the reliability of Alzheimer's blood tests
mix_items.summary: Researchers at University Medicine Halle have developed a new method that could improve the reliability of blood tests for Alzheimer's disease. Current commercial tests often rely on the protein biomarker p-tau217, whose levels can rise in the early stages of the disease. However, the biomarker levels can also be elevated in other conditions, potentially leading to false-positive results. In a study involving 315 participants, the research team demonstrated improved accuracy in distinguishing Alzheimer's disease from other conditions. Their findings have been published in Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: Location of rare cancer impacts survival, study suggests
mix_items.summary: A rare, aggressive cancer, commonly found in the uterus, limbs and abdomen, behaves differently depending on where it is found in the body, according to new research.

mix_items.title: Viagra's cousin could help muscle cells stay primed for regeneration
mix_items.summary: Tadalafil is a prescription drug closely related to Viagra. It is used to treat erectile dysfunction (ED) and the urinary symptoms of an enlarged prostate. Both competitive and recreational athletes sometimes use it too, to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), a condition that can limit how well the body tolerates exercise.

During summer 2026, the SEES Mission Architecture Tool for Research, Integration, and eXploration (MATRIX) team […]

mix_items.title: Hidden chromosome structures reveal greater complexity in how roundworms organize DNA
mix_items.summary: Almost every cell in our body contains around two meters (6.6 feet) of DNA, packed into a tiny nucleus. Yet for the cell to function, this enormous amount of genetic material must remain organized and accessible. Researchers at the University of Basel have now discovered three distinct types of large chromosomal domains that help organize DNA in nuclei.

mix_items.title: The power of poop: Why conservationists love animal scat
mix_items.summary: I never thought my shoelaces would get stolen.

mix_items.title: One violin lesson changes brain wave patterns as beginners learn to play
mix_items.summary: A new study using wearable brain imaging has shown what happens in the human brain when someone learns to play a musical instrument. The results revealed the patterns of brain activity that enable us to play an instrument, in this case a violin, and how having just a single lesson significantly changes those patterns of activity.

mix_items.title: AI-powered robotic laboratory paves the way for discovering next-generation heat-resistant coatings
mix_items.summary: Researchers have developed a self-driving laboratory that combines artificial intelligence and robotics to automate laboratory tasks, from accurately measuring and mixing chemical ingredients to high-temperature furnace processing and sample retrieval.

mix_items.title: Two distinct sleep stages emerge in jumping spider, including a REM-like state
mix_items.summary: Humans and other vertebrates go through various stages of sleep, including REM (rapid eye movement) sleep characterized by rapid eye movements and muscle twitches. Can a similar sleep state be observed in spiders? Researchers from the Institute of Organismic Biology at the University of Bonn investigated this in the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata. The work is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

mix_items.title: New treatment approach shows promise in reducing prostate cancer spread
mix_items.summary: Adding darolutamide to standard treatment for aggressive prostate cancer reduced the risk of the disease spreading in an international phase 3 trial.

mix_items.title: Fructose slows liver tumors in mice when key sugar-processing gene is missing, may lead to new treatments
mix_items.summary: Fructose is an important nutrient that, despite having a chemical structure very similar to that of glucose, is metabolized very differently in the body. Research into fructose metabolism and its regulation of metabolism in the human body has in recent years become a frontier topic in the life sciences and medicine. A new study led by researchers at City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK) has found that in the specific metabolic context of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), dietary fructose does not fuel tumor growth. Instead, it can suppress it, revealing a previously unknown anticancer mechanism.

mix_items.title: Previously unrecognized immune cells may drive harmful blood vessel growth in blinding eye diseases
mix_items.summary: A Northwestern Medicine study has identified a previously unrecognized population of immune cells that appears to fuel harmful blood vessel growth in multiple blinding eye diseases, according to the study published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation. The discovery could open the door to new treatments for patients who don't respond to existing therapies, said the study's senior author Jeremy Lavine, M.D., Ph.D., assistant professor of ophthalmology.

mix_items.title: Immunotherapy combo extends survival for patients with aggressive small cell lung cancer, based on trial results
mix_items.summary: In patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC), tarlatamab, a bispecific T-cell engager, plus durvalumab as first-line maintenance therapy extended median overall survival by more than eight months, more than tripled progression-free survival and reduced the risk of death by 58% compared to durvalumab alone, according to results of the phase 3 open-label, multicenter, randomized DeLLphi-305 study.

mix_items.title: Florida dengue cases nearly double a month after emergency declared
mix_items.summary: Dengue cases in Florida keep climbing about a month after three counties declared states of emergency over the mosquito-borne illness.

mix_items.title: AI chatbots may worsen symptoms in people with psychosis
mix_items.summary: Conversational AI chatbots are a relatively new technology, but they are now ubiquitous, embedded in everything from customer service platforms to personal productivity tools. Such is their rapid adoption that potential negative consequences are yet to be fully understood.

mix_items.title: AI chatbots can be a valuable health resource for older adults—if they embrace 'informed skepticism'
mix_items.summary: It's easy to stereotype older adults as tech-averse or novice tech users. Yet a growing number of adults age 60 and older are embracing artificial intelligence, using it for entertainment, planning trips and even accessing health information.

mix_items.title: Governors allied with Flávio Bolsonaro set to lead majority of Brazilian Amazon states
mix_items.summary: Seven of Brazil’s nine Amazonian states are set to be governed by politicians aligned with far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, Lucas Berti reported for Mongabay Brasil. On Oct. 25, Brazil will have an electoral face-off between the top two candidates for several races that were not able to secure more than 50% of the vote in […]

mix_items.title: Inside the ‘unique’ tail of Iran’s spider-tailed horned viper
mix_items.summary: The Iranian spider-tailed horned viper, a rare snake endemic to western Iran, hunts by holding its body completely still while twitching its tail. Its body camouflages among the rocks of its semi-arid Zagros Mountains habitat, but its bulbous tail with accompanying leg-like scales looks remarkably like a large chunky spider. The snake, Pseudocerastes urarachnoides, uses its […]

mix_items.title: As sand becomes more valuable, Sierra Leone’s Mahera Coast grows more vulnerable
mix_items.summary: PORT LOKO, Sierra Leone — When the tide pulls away from the beach in the agricultural regions in Mahera in Lungi, about 27 kilometers (17 miles) across the sea from the country’s capital, Freetown, the digging commences. Young men shovel sand into cement bags and carry them to a flat open area to pile sand […]

mix_items.title: New Zealand builds an arsenal of tools to battle a ‘wily’ invasive seaweed
mix_items.summary: BAY OF ISLANDS, Aotearoa New Zealand — Since an invasive seaweed called caulerpa was discovered in Aotearoa New Zealand in 2021, forming meadows that blanketed parts of the seabed, it’s taken on an almost mythical status among people who spend time in coastal waters. “It’s so wily and so resilient,” Michele Rogalin-Henderson, a doctoral candidate […]

mix_items.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea
mix_items.summary: COLOMBO – Sri Lanka’s spectacled cobra (Naja naja) carries a two-million-year-old genetic mystery, and a new study finds that the island’s cobras form a genetically distinct lineage, reopening a taxonomic question raised by a Sri Lankan zoologist nearly nine decades ago. The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

mix_items.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
mix_items.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

mix_items.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
mix_items.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

mix_items.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
mix_items.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

mix_items.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
mix_items.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

mix_items.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.
